payload.previous_feedback: Previous vetter reason: The proof directly establishes the stated decomposition of an arbitrary real number into its integer part and fractional part, and correctly verifies 0 <= frac(x) < 1. It matches the lemma exactly and uses only standard floor/fractional-part definitions.
payload.previous_proof_nl: Let x be any real number. By definition of the floor function, m := floor(x) is an integer such that m <= x < m + 1. Define f := x - m. Then f >= 0 because x >= m, and f < 1 because x < m + 1. By the usual definition of the fractional part, frac(x) = x - floor(x) = x - m = f. Therefore x = m + f = floor(x) + frac(x), and also 0 <= frac(x) < 1. Since x was arbitrary, the statement holds for every real number x.
payload.role_in_assembly: Provide the canonical decomposition of an arbitrary real number into an integer part and a fractional part.

result_payload.proof_nl: Let x be any real number. Set m = floor(x). By the defining property of the floor function, m is an integer with m <= x < m + 1. Define f = x - m. Then f >= 0, since x >= m, and f < 1, since x < m + 1. By the standard definition of the fractional part, frac(x) = x - floor(x) = x - m = f. Therefore x = m + f = floor(x) + frac(x), and also 0 <= frac(x) < 1. Since x was arbitrary, the statement holds for every real number x.
result_payload.proof_summary: For arbitrary real x, write m=floor(x) and f=x-m. The floor inequality gives 0<=f<1, and the fractional part is x-floor(x)=f. Hence x=floor(x)+frac(x) with 0<=frac(x)<1.
